section_summary: This section continues a book-length study of modern Japan, covering industrial development, dependence on imported raw materials, concentrated family-controlled enterprises, and the conditions of factory and household labor. It then examines rural poverty, tenancy, taxation, agricultural policy, emigration, and the conservative influence of the family system, Shinto, schools, police, and youth associations. The final pages begin a chapter on the coexistence of traditional and Western practices in Japanese cities, journalism, sports, entertainment, and women’s lives.

subfiles.title: Study of Modern Japan, Chapters 7–9: Industrial Conditions, Farmers, and Conflicting Currents
subfiles.about: A continued analytical study of Japan’s industrial economy, labor conditions, agrarian problems, conservative rural institutions, and tensions between traditional and Western culture.
subfiles.summary: Chapter 7 traces Japan’s industrial growth after 1895, its dependence on imported minerals, petroleum, and cotton, and the concentration of finance and industry in family-controlled combines such as Mitsui. It describes low wages, long hours, paternalistic factory discipline, female and child labor, household production, silk reeling, and the weakness and official control of organized labor. Chapter 8 analyzes small farms, discriminatory taxation, tenancy, debt, rice policy, immigration, and the ways family organization, Shinto, education, police supervision, and youth associations sustain rural conservatism. Chapter 9 begins by illustrating the coexistence of Japanese and Western forms in urban life, newspapers, sports, theater, music, and women’s activities.
